title: Adam's du'a
hookLine: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves (7:23)

lines: NOT MY FAULT, OR THAT WAS ME?
cards: A plate in pieces on the kitchen floor, and two people standing over it. Before anyone reaches for a broom, somebody speaks. Two sentences are always waiting in that moment.
It wasn't my fault. Or: that was me. In the Qur'an's garden story, two creatures get something badly wrong, and each reaches for one of those sentences.
One argues his case. The other, Adam, with his wife beside him, turns his sentence into a prayer.

teach.b: Surah al-A'raf tells it. Iblis is commanded to bow to Adam and refuses. His reason: I am better than him; You made me from fire and him from clay.
Later, sent out, he says: because You have led me astray. Blame upward, blame outward. Then Adam and his wife eat from the tree they'd been told to leave alone.

And in verse twenty-three, in Pickthall's translation: "They said: Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If Thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!" Three things. First, they.
Both pray it together; the Qur'an doesn't put the blame on her. Second, ourselves. Not Satan, who whispered to them, not the tree, not each other.

The wrong is named as damage done to their own souls. Third, the request is only forgiveness and mercy, with nothing bargained. Al-Baqarah says Adam received words from his Lord, and Allah turned to him in forgiveness.
Some commentators say those words were this very prayer: Allah taught Adam how to come back, and then accepted it. In Islamic teaching, that forgiveness closed the matter.
The Qur'an says no soul carries another's burden, so Adam's children are each born free of his slip. The garden story ends, in the Qur'an, not with a curse but with a returned prayer.
Du'a, the word for this kind of personal prayer, means a call. Adam's call is three words long at its heart: rabbana zalamna anfusana.

how: Muslims learn Adam's du'a (7:23) as one of the Qur'an's prayers for forgiveness; some say it in the prostration or after the prayer.

o: a prayer to go back to the garden at once
our Lord, we have wronged ourselves
a plea that blames Satan for the slip

s: in the Qur'an, the blame falls on Adam's wife
they pray together, and the Qur'an doesn't put the blame on her.
some commentators say Allah taught Adam this prayer
2:37: Adam received words from his Lord, and some read them as 7:23.
in Islamic teaching, Adam's children inherit his sin
the Qur'an says no soul carries another's burden.

games.q: you're Adam. you and your wife have eaten from the tree. what do you say?
o: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.
Iblis tricked us; it was him.
games.why: they own it together, ask only for forgiveness and mercy, and Allah turns to them (7:23; 2:37).

practice: Let one recent wrong of yours come to mind, small is fine, and notice the excuse that usually comes with it; set the excuse down beside you.
If you pray, say Adam's words once, slowly: rabbana zalamna anfusana, our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If not, say the plain version to yourself: that was mine.

wordCard.voice: Adam's du'a. Rabbana zalamna anfusana: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. A prayer that owns the wrong, answered with forgiveness. Today's word.
